title: Joshua 15:20–63
context: After the borders comes the inventory: Judah's towns grouped by region, from the Negev (the South) toward Edom, through the lowland (Shephelah) and the Philistine coast, up into the hill country around Hebron, and down into the wilderness by the Dead Sea. Many of these places return in the stories of the patriarchs, the judges, David, and the prophets. The chapter closes with a candid note that Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem.

verses.text: This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Judah according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes: "This is the inheritance" introduces the town list. Arminian readers see inheritance language as covenant gift: the land is not earned by Judah, yet it is entrusted to them as a stewardship to be lived out faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the heading as a record of what God has apportioned. Like the psalmist's "The LORD assigned my portion and my cup" (Psalm 16:5), Judah's towns are received as God's settled gift.

verses.text: The farthest cities of the tribe of the children of Judah toward the border of Edom in the South were Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur,
verses.arminianNotes: The list begins at the far south "toward the border of Edom." Arminian readers note that even the dry fringe of the Negev is part of the gift, inviting Israel to trust God's provision in hard terrain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God's ordering reach to the margins of the land. The inheritance is defined from edge to edge by God's word, not by where Israel already feels strong or settled.

verses.arminianNotes: Kinah, Dimonah, and Adadah are little-known towns. Arminian readers note that the text honors obscure places alongside famous ones, a reminder that God's promises take in ordinary lives and communities.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in names otherwise unknown a quiet witness to providence. God's care is not limited to places that make headlines; every village in the inheritance is named under his oversight.

verses.arminianNotes: Kedesh, Hazor, and Ithnan share names with places elsewhere in Israel; these are southern towns. Arminian readers see the list as a call to remember where God planted his people and to live there in covenant loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that repeated place names across the land remind us these lists are records, not inventions. God fulfills his promise in concrete, mapped detail rather than vague generalities.

verses.arminianNotes: Ziph here is a southern town, distinct from the Ziph in verse 55. Arminian readers find in the careful record a God who keeps faith with his people at the level of names and places, inviting their trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the precision of the list as an expression of God's faithfulness. What he promised to Abraham's offspring is now itemized town by town, a sign that none of his words fall to the ground.

verses.text: Hazor Hadattah, Kerioth Hezron (also called Hazor),
verses.arminianNotes: Hazor Hadattah and Kerioth Hezron (also called Hazor) are southern settlements. Arminian readers note that the inheritance includes small and remote places, each one entrusted to families who must hold it faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's allotment is comprehensive. The record does not skip the remote settlements, because the whole land belongs to God and he distributes all of it to his people.

verses.arminianNotes: Moladah reappears in Simeon's list (Joshua 19:2), since Simeon's portion lay within Judah's. Arminian readers see tribes called to share their gift, living out mutual responsibility within the covenant people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note Joshua 19:9: Simeon received land within Judah "for the portion of the children of Judah was too much for them." God's distribution provides for the whole people, not one tribe alone.

verses.arminianNotes: Hazar Gaddah, Heshmon, and Beth Pelet are Negev settlements. Arminian readers note that the list moves place by place, reflecting a God who meets his people in the specific locations where they are called to live.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God's sovereign apportionment reaching each settlement. Even unfamiliar names stand as testimony that God's covenant purposes are carried out in real history, one town at a time.

verses.arminianNotes: Beersheba was named for the oath sworn there in Abraham's day (Genesis 21:31). Arminian readers see the patriarch's place of covenant-making now held by his descendants, a promise met by a people called to trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how a site tied to Abraham's life returns as part of Judah's inheritance and is listed again for Simeon (Joshua 19:2). God's promise to the fathers is kept to their children.

verses.arminianNotes: Baalah, Iim, and Ezem continue the southern list. Arminian readers note that some towns carry names linked to Canaanite worship, a reminder that Israel was called to faithfulness in a land shaped by other gods.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God gives his people places once shaped by other worship. The land is cleansed and claimed for the LORD by his gift, and the people must not return to the gods it once served.

verses.arminianNotes: Hormah, a name related to the word for devotion to destruction, recalls Numbers 21:3, where God heard Israel's vow and "delivered up the Canaanites." Arminian readers see answered prayer and covenant response bound together in that memory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the name as a memorial of God's judgment and of his giving victory. The towns of the inheritance carry the history of God's acts, reminding Israel that the land is held by grace.

verses.arminianNotes: Ziklag later became David's base, given to him by the Philistine king Achish (1 Samuel 27:6). Arminian readers note that places assigned now become settings for later choices, both faithful and compromised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note 1 Samuel 27:6: "Ziklag belongs to the kings of Judah to this day." A town listed here returns to Judah's royal line through a winding providence, showing God steering history toward his king.

verses.text: Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon. All the cities are twenty-nine, with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: The names listed number more than the stated "twenty-nine," and interpreters explain the difference in various ways. Arminian readers see no need to force a solution; the text faithfully preserves the record as received.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the text in high regard while acknowledging the counting question. Proposed explanations include compound names counted as one; the main point, God's complete provision, stands either way.

verses.text: In the lowland, Eshtaol, Zorah, Ashnah,
verses.arminianNotes: The second region is "the lowland," the foothills toward the coast. Eshtaol and Zorah later frame Samson's story (Judges 13:25). Arminian readers see the land as the stage for Israel's real struggles of faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how these lowland towns become sites of God's deliverance in Judges. The allotment lays out ahead of time the places where God will later raise up deliverers by his Spirit.

verses.arminianNotes: Zanoah, En Gannim, Tappuah, and Enam continue the lowland group. Arminian readers note that inheritance is communal and generational, with towns and "villages" held by families who must keep covenant together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see these names as part of God's ordered distribution. The same God who chose Israel also places families in particular towns, binding his promise to the ordinary settings of daily life.

verses.arminianNotes: Adullam later sheltered David in "Adullam's cave" (1 Samuel 22:1), and the Philistines camped "between Socoh and Azekah" before Goliath (1 Samuel 17:1). Arminian readers see future faith tested on this ground.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers trace God's providence through these places: the valley of David's victory over Goliath and the refuge of his exile. God's purposes for his anointed are rooted in the inheritance assigned here.

verses.text: Shaaraim, Adithaim and Gederah (or Gederothaim); fourteen cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: The group is totaled as "fourteen cities with their villages," with Gederah given an alternate name. Arminian readers see the summaries as accountability: the gift is known and counted, to be held faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the tallies as a ledger of grace. God's provision is not vague; it is counted and recorded, a reassurance that he has given exactly what he promised to the tribe.

verses.arminianNotes: Zenan, Hadashah, and Migdal Gad begin another lowland group. Arminian readers note that the list's district structure suggests an orderly community life, a framework within which Israel could serve God faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's gifts come with order. Land divided into districts and towns reflects a God of order who provides structure for his people's life together under his rule.

verses.arminianNotes: Dilean, Mizpah, and Joktheel continue the group; this Mizpah is a lowland town, not the better-known Mizpah of Benjamin. Arminian readers see each name as part of a gift Israel must receive and keep in faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the repeated common names a reminder of how widely God's people were spread through the land. Each settlement, however small, falls within the inheritance God gives.

verses.arminianNotes: Lachish and Eglon were among the cities whose kings joined against Gibeon and whom Joshua defeated (Joshua 10:3, 32). Arminian readers see past victories turned into homes, a call to keep trusting the God who fought for them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that "The LORD delivered Lachish into the hand of Israel" (Joshua 10:32). The towns that once opposed Israel are now its inheritance, a sign that God himself gives the victory and the land.

verses.arminianNotes: Cabbon, Lahmam, and Chitlish are otherwise little known. Arminian readers find encouragement that God's word preserves the names of places most readers have never heard of, showing his care for every community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see these obscure names as a reminder that Scripture records God's faithfulness in detail. No part of the inheritance is too small to be included in his ordered giving.

verses.text: Gederoth, Beth Dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah; sixteen cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Makkedah, where Joshua's southern campaign turned (Joshua 10:29), closes this group of "sixteen cities." Arminian readers see conquered sites become settled towns, a gift to be held by continued obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the places of God's victories become the places of his people's rest. The campaign of Joshua 10 bears fruit in towns now allotted to Judah's families by God's assignment.

verses.arminianNotes: Libnah, also taken in Joshua 10:29, begins another group. Arminian readers note that the allotment draws on the history of God's help, encouraging Israel to live in grateful dependence rather than self-reliance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Libnah another fulfilled word. What God won for Israel in battle he now distributes, and the inheritance stands as a lasting witness that the victory was his.

verses.arminianNotes: Iphtah, Ashnah, and Nezib continue the lowland list; Ashnah also appears in verse 33, likely a second town of that name. Arminian readers note that duplicate names show the record was kept carefully, not smoothed over.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the text preserves such details without explanation. God's word is faithful to the real record, and readers can trust the main point: God has given Judah a full inheritance.

verses.text: Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah; nine cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Keilah, which David later rescued from the Philistines (1 Samuel 23:1), and Achzib and Mareshah, named in Micah 1:14–15, close this group. Arminian readers see these places become stages of faith and failure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Micah later pronounces judgment on Achzib and Mareshah. Towns given in grace can later face discipline for unfaithfulness, a reminder that God's gifts call for covenant loyalty.

verses.text: Ekron, with its towns and its villages;
verses.arminianNotes: Ekron, a Philistine city, is assigned to Judah "with its towns and its villages." Arminian readers note that some allotments describe land still to be taken, calling for faith that acts on God's promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Judges 1:18 says Judah later took Ekron, while Judges 1:19 records limits to the conquest. The allotment states God's grant; its possession unfolds over time under his hand.

verses.text: from Ekron even to the sea, all that were by the side of Ashdod, with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: The district runs "from Ekron even to the sea" alongside Ashdod. Arminian readers see an invitation to trust that God's word reaches even the strongholds of Israel's enemies, while Israel's response remains real.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God assigning territory that, from a human view, still belonged to the Philistines. His word marks out the inheritance before it is secured, much as he named the land to Abraham long before.

verses.text: Ashdod, its towns and its villages; Gaza, its towns and its villages; to the brook of Egypt, and the great sea with its coastline.
verses.arminianNotes: Ashdod and Gaza reach "to the brook of Egypt." Arminian readers note that the Philistine coast long remained contested, showing that Israel's enjoyment of the gift depended on continued faithful action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the prophets later announce judgment on these same cities (Zephaniah 2:4). God remains Lord over the Philistine coast, and his purposes for it are carried out in his time.

verses.text: In the hill country, Shamir, Jattir, Socoh,
verses.arminianNotes: "In the hill country" begins the third region. This Socoh is a different town from the lowland one in verse 35. Arminian readers see Judah's heartland given as a place to live out covenant faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the hill country, where Judah was strongest (Judges 1:19), is the core of its inheritance. God places his people securely while still leaving room for future growth in possession.

verses.arminianNotes: "Kiriath Sannah (which is Debir)" gives another name for the city Othniel captured (verses 15–17). Arminian readers see the story of Caleb's family faith tied to a real town on Judah's map.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the place won through Othniel's courage is fixed in the official list. God's gift to Caleb's household becomes part of Judah's lasting inheritance, just as he promised.

verses.arminianNotes: Anab, Eshtemoh, and Anim are hill-country towns. Arminian readers note that Anab appears in Joshua 11:21 among places from which the Anakim were cut off, a reminder of how fear once gave way to faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in such towns the result of God's victory over the Anakim, whom earlier Israel feared. What seemed impossible at Kadesh Barnea is now an ordinary entry in the town list, by God's power.

verses.text: Goshen, Holon, and Giloh; eleven cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Goshen, Holon, and Giloh close a group of "eleven cities." This Goshen is a town in Judah, not the region in Egypt. Arminian readers see each tally as a reminder of the gift's completeness and the call to keep it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God provides in full measure. Each summary count closes a section of the inheritance with a sense of completeness, testifying to God's faithful and orderly provision.

verses.arminianNotes: Arab, Dumah, and Eshan open another hill-country group. Arminian readers note that the list is a testimony for later generations, calling them to remember that their homes were received from God, not seized by their own strength.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as a memorial of grace for every later generation of Judah. The towns where families lived were assigned by God, so their whole life there rested on his giving.

verses.arminianNotes: Janim, Beth Tappuah, and Aphekah continue the group. Arminian readers find in these ordinary names a picture of a covenant that touches the whole of life: fields, villages, and the work of daily living.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's sovereignty is not abstract but reaches into the details of where families live. These modest settlements are as much part of his plan as the famous cities.

verses.text: Humtah, Kiriath Arba (also called Hebron), and Zior; nine cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Kiriath Arba, "also called Hebron," was where Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob lived as foreigners (Genesis 35:27). Arminian readers see the patriarchs' hope realized in their descendants, a promise met by faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David later reigned in Hebron "over Judah seven years and six months" (2 Samuel 5:5). The patriarchs' place of sojourning becomes the first seat of Judah's king, a thread of providence.

verses.arminianNotes: Maon, Carmel, and Ziph later appear in David's years of flight from Saul (1 Samuel 23:14; 25:2). Arminian readers see future choices of loyalty and betrayal played out in these hill-country towns.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that "God didn't deliver him into his hand" (1 Samuel 23:14) while David hid in the wilderness of Ziph. God preserved his anointed in places he had long ago assigned to Judah.

verses.arminianNotes: Jezreel, Jokdeam, and Zanoah continue the group; this Jezreel is a Judean town, not the northern valley. Arminian readers see the record as an encouragement to trust a God who keeps faith in specific places.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how often place names repeat across Israel and how carefully the text keeps them distinct. God's word preserves an accurate record of the inheritance he gave his people.

verses.text: Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah; ten cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah close a group of "ten cities." These are hill-country towns, distinct from places of the same names elsewhere. Arminian readers see the tally as a call to faithful stewardship of a counted gift.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the tally as another testimony to God's complete giving. Every group is summed up, so Judah could know that its inheritance was full, exact, and sure.

verses.arminianNotes: Halhul, Beth Zur, and Gedor lie in the hill country. Arminian readers note that God's gift includes defensible towns and farmland alike, and that Israel's security would rest finally on faithfulness to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God providing both shelter and sustenance for his people. Whatever the strategic value of these towns, Judah's true security lay in the God who gave them.

verses.text: Maarath, Beth Anoth, and Eltekon; six cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Maarath, Beth Anoth, and Eltekon close a group of "six cities." The Greek translation adds a further group of towns after this verse, including Bethlehem; the Hebrew followed here does not have it. Arminian readers simply note the difference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note this textual difference without resolving it. Whichever text is original, the passage's teaching is unaffected: God has given Judah a complete and ordered inheritance.

verses.text: Kiriath Baal (also called Kiriath Jearim), and Rabbah; two cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Kiriath Baal (also called Kiriath Jearim) and Rabbah form a group of two. Kiriath Jearim later housed the ark (1 Samuel 7:1). Arminian readers see a place where God's presence would be honored or neglected by later choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the ark stayed at Kiriath Jearim until David brought it up (1 Chronicles 13:6). A border town listed here becomes part of God's unfolding plan for his presence in Jerusalem.

verses.text: In the wilderness, Beth Arabah, Middin, Secacah,
verses.arminianNotes: "In the wilderness" introduces the final region, the dry land west of the Dead Sea. Arminian readers note that even barren ground is included, calling Israel to trust God's provision where life is hardest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God's gift extending to the wilderness. The God who sustained Israel in the desert also assigns desert towns, and his care covers every corner of the land.

verses.text: Nibshan, the City of Salt, and En Gedi; six cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Nibshan, the City of Salt, and En Gedi complete the list. David later hid "in the wilderness of En Gedi" (1 Samuel 24:1). Arminian readers see this oasis become a scene of costly mercy and choices of faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that at En Gedi, God kept David safe and David spared Saul (1 Samuel 24). The final town on the list points ahead to God's protection of his chosen king in the wilderness.

verses.text: As for the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah couldn’t drive them out; but the Jebusites live with the children of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah "couldn't drive them out." Judges 1:21 says the same of Benjamin, whose list also includes Jerusalem (Joshua 18:28). Arminian readers see real human failure: the gift was sure, but its full enjoyment required faithful obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hold the failure to be real and culpable, while noting that David later "took the stronghold of Zion" (2 Samuel 5:7). What Judah could not do then, God accomplished later through his chosen king.
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions hold that God's promise was faithful (Joshua 21:45) and Israel's failure was real. Arminian readers stress that the full enjoyment of the promise was conditioned on Israel's faithful response. Reformed readers stress that God's purpose for Jerusalem was not thwarted, and that he brought it to pass through David in his own time.
